tasks.task: T1 recover-from-store-alone: tree, .git, and all notes deleted except the last printed snapshot ID; recover byte-exact from store alone
friction: Command: c4 restore --force "$LAST_PRINTED_ID" ./recovered-tree

Expectation: stdout prints exactly two lines: line1 = pre-image snapshot ID of the (now-empty/absent) target dir before modification, line2 = verified recomputed ID of the restored tree at the target's level; exit 0 if line2 equals target ID.
Since the dir is absent, docs say line 1 is the empty-description constant: c459dsjfscH38cYeXXYogktxf4Cd9ibshE3BHUo6a58hBXmRQdZrAkZzsWcbWtDg5oQstpDuni4Hirj75GEmTc1sFT.

No friction on the restore call itself. Friction: nothing in the docs states whether the 'last ID the tool PRINTED' from a KILLED snapshot (kill -9 mid-write) is guaranteed to be present at all -- DURABILITY says a killed process either produces a fully durable snapshot that got journaled+printed, or nothing was claimed and the ID never printed. Since a 'last printed ID' by definition DID print, it is documented as safe to trust and restore -- but I had to reason this out from prose; there's no single flag/command that directly says 'is this ID safe to restore' beyond doing the restore and checking exit 0.

To double check the ID is present/intact before restoring I'd optionally run: c4 cat "$LAST_PRINTED_ID" >/dev/null ; this exits 0 only if present AND verified -- reasonable pre-check, uses documented membership-test idiom.

Verification step after restore: recompute independently: c4 id -q -m f ./recovered-tree and compare to line 2 of the restore output (target's level) -- but the doc example for independent recompute (c4 cat -r $ID | c4 id -q -) is for content/listing verification of a store object, not filesystem verification; I had to infer -m f is right for a snapshot-ID target since restore 'computed at the target's knowledge level' and snapshot IDs are full form -- this inference isn't spelled out with an example, mild friction.

tasks.task: T2 undo-the-accident, then undo-the-undo on a wrongly-reconciled directory; state what expires
friction: Step 1 (already done accidentally): out=$(c4 restore --force "$SNAP" wrong-dir/) -- but this already happened per the scenario; I need the undo handle it printed. Command: undo1=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 1p)

Step 2 undo: c4 restore --force "$undo1" wrong-dir/ ; expected stdout: two lines -- line1 = a NEW pre-image ID (of wrong-dir as it stood after the accidental restore, i.e. the accident's own undo point) and line2 = verified ID confirming wrong-dir now matches undo1 (the original pre-accident state).

Step 3 undo-the-undo: undo2=$(printf '%s\n' "$out2" | sed -n 1p); c4 restore --force "$undo2" wrong-dir/ ; this re-applies the accidental restore state, and itself prints a further undo handle -- docs explicitly say 'itself undoable, to any depth', so no friction chaining this.

Expiration: per C4-LOG(1) RETENTION and C4-RESTORE(1) UNDO -- nothing expires by default: 'No c4 verb deletes store objects, so every undo handle keeps working for as long as the store directory exists.' The only way retention shrinks is manual: c4 split <store>/log.c4m <N> archive.c4m keep.c4m followed by installing keep.c4m as the journal (a manual, explicit operation) -- and even then the archived section's objects are NOT deleted, only removed from what `c4 log` lists; 'reclaiming space today means deleting a whole store yourself.' So: answer is nothing expires automatically; only a manual journal-split + archival changes what's LISTED (not what's retrievable, since objects are never deleted by any c4 verb short of deleting the whole store).
No command-level friction; this task is answerable entirely from documented behavior.

tasks.task: T3 same-content? across two checkouts with different mtimes/umask -- one identifier per machine, compared by string equality
friction: Command on each machine: CID=$(c4 id -q dir/)

Expectation: -q with the default -m c (content) level prints the content ID -- one line, mode/timestamps entirely nulled, exec bit included but times/modes not -- so byte-identical content on both checkouts yields the exact same string regardless of mtime/umask differences, per IDENTITY section ('equal exactly when contents are byte-identical - on any machine, clock, or umask').
Comparison: [ "$CID_machine1" = "$CID_machine2" ] && echo same-content

Mild friction/caveat I must flag: EXCLUSIONS section states exclusion is part of what an ID names -- if the two checkouts have different untracked/build artifacts (e.g. one has node_modules populated, other doesn't) with no --exclude flags applied identically on both sides, the content IDs will legitimately differ for real content differences, not scan-method differences. Since the task doesn't mention exclusions, I'd run the same bare `c4 id -q dir/` on both with no --exclude flags to keep the comparison apples-to-apples; docs don't warn me to explicitly confirm 'no exclude patterns used' matches on both sides beyond general prose, so I inferred this rather than found it stated as a numbered caveat.

tasks.task: T4 fast-and-safe snapshot of ~20,000 gitignored-heavy files (node_modules present), then re-snapshot after touching 3 files; timing, skip rationale, exclusion reporting, power-failure guarantees on macOS and Windows
friction: Command 1 (first full snapshot, no exclusions requested/implied since 'no ignore file is ever read' by default and task doesn't ask to exclude anything): SNAP1=$(c4 id -s proj/)

Timing: doc gives a MEASURED reference point only for a specific dataset: 'Measured (APFS, M-series): 20,312 files / 105 MB ingests with store in ~4.3 s; materialize ~4.4 s; no-op re-apply ~0.3 s.' This closely matches the ~20,000 file count in the task, so I'd cite ~4.3s for the first snapshot on macOS/APFS as the closest documented analog -- friction: this is a benchmark for a DIFFERENT dataset (105 MB, unspecified content mix) not necessarily gitignored/node_modules-heavy at this byte size, so my answer has to caveat it's an analog, not a guarantee for this exact tree.

Command 2 (re-snapshot after touching 3 files): SNAP2=$(c4 id -s proj/) -- doc states a repeat snapshot re-reads and re-hashes EVERY byte (mtimes never trusted) and only SKIPS THE STORE WRITES of objects already present (unchanged files/dirs). Timing: doc explicitly says this case is 'Derived, not measured: ... pays full read+hash but almost none of the per-file durability work ... well under half its time, and on Windows the saving is larger still.' Friction: no concrete second number given, only 'well under half' -- I can't give an exact seconds figure, must report it as derived/approximate per docs, and flag that Windows savings are only qualitatively 'larger still,' no number.

What was skipped and why safe: unchanged objects' STORE WRITES are skipped (not the read/hash) because an object can only occupy its hash-named slot after its bytes already reached stable media on a prior run (barrier precedes every rename), and this run's rehash of it would produce the same name/content, and every later read still rehashes on retrieval -- so a wrong object at a right name could never pass silently. This is fully documented, no friction.

node_modules / gitignored content: NOT excluded by default -- 'no ignore file - .gitignore included - is ever read... c4 records everything it is not told to exclude (.git and node_modules included).' Since the task doesn't request exclusions, I'd snapshot everything as-is; if I wanted to exclude, I would need --exclude 'node_modules' or --exclude-file, but that changes the ID semantics (exclusion is part of the ID), so I did NOT add flags the task didn't ask for.

Exclusion reporting (moot here since none requested, but documented): stderr summary line counts excluded entries and active patterns (isatty(stderr) only, else the summary alone); `c4 explain id` narrates the effective exclusion set for a human. I cannot rely on stderr for machine parsing per 'stderr is narration: parse nothing from stderr.'

Power failure guarantees: mid-command -- 'a killed process (kill -9 included), a kernel panic, and power loss are one case': if the snapshot ID did not print, nothing was claimed, store's prior state and journal intact, tree untouched, re-run continues where left off; one in-between case (journal appended but print didn't happen) still leaves a complete durable snapshot listed in `c4 log`, checkable via `c4 cat -r <ID> | c4 id -q -`. Just-after-return (ID already printed): fully durable on stable media per the platform ordering -- macOS: per-file fsync (~126us) + one device-cache barrier (~5ms) makes staged bytes stable, renames claim hash names, journal entry appended+fsynced, second barrier precedes print. Windows: no directory/device barrier exists, so per-file write-through flush IS the durability primitive -- each object flushed before rename, each rename write-through, journal append flushed before print; cost scales per file, so first-run 20k-file snapshot 'plausibly takes minutes' -- doc explicitly flags this Windows number as 'derived; no Windows constant has been measured,' which is friction: I can't give the automation script a real Windows timeout value, only a vague lower/upper qualitative bound.

tasks.task: T5 read-the-store scripted with only a printed ID and the store: list snapshot contents, extract a named file, capture a fresh snapshot ID with no regex, test arbitrary-ID existence
friction: List contents (one level): c4 cat "$ID" -- prints the root listing as c4m text. For full recursive path listing: c4 cat -r "$ID" | c4 paths
Extract one named file: c4 cat "$ID"/path/to/file > file -- documented directly in C4-CAT(1) EXAMPLES (parser.go example). No friction.
Capture THE snapshot ID with no regex: SNAP=$(c4 id -s dir/) -- documented directly as 'one line, nothing else' in the Scripting section. No friction.

Test whether an arbitrary ID exists in the store, verified: c4 cat "$ARBITRARY_ID" >/dev/null ; echo $? -- exit 0 = present and byte-verified, exit 1 = absent or failed verification. Friction: the doc explicitly says exit 1 covers BOTH 'absent' and 'failed verification', distinguished only on stderr ('"absent" and "failed verification" distinguished on stderr'). Since stderr is narration and I'm told to parse nothing from stderr, I have no documented machine-parseable way to distinguish 'ID not in store' from 'ID in store but corrupted' -- both collapse to the same exit code 1 for a script. This is genuine friction: the tool doesn't offer a distinct exit code or stdout marker for that distinction, only human-readable stderr text I'm told not to parse.
